item.title: Go Daily Question 152
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

func main() {
    var x = []int{4: 44, 55, 66, 1: 77, 88}
    println(len(x), x[2])
}
  • A: 5 66
  • B: 5 88
  • C: 7 88
  • D: None of the above
🔑 Answer Analysis:

C Run online

In Go, slices/arrays can be initialized with indices.

// 1. Elements without keys
slice1 := []int{1, 2, 3}

// 2. Elements with keys (keys are indices)
slice2 := []string{0: "a", 1: "b", 2: "c"}

This problem uses a mixed initialization method with explicit and implicit indices.

item.title: Go Daily Question 151
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import (
    "fmt"
)

func main() {
    a := []int{2: 1}
    fmt.Println(a)
}
  • A: Compilation error;
  • B: [2 1];
  • C: [0 0 1];
  • D: [0 1]
🔑 Answer Analysis:

C Run online

In Go, slices/arrays can be initialized with indices.

// 1. Elements without keys
slice1 := []int{1, 2, 3}

// 2. Elements with keys (keys are indices)
slice2 := []string{0: "a", 1: "b", 2: "c"}

In this problem, it means the element at index 2 is 1, so the slice content is [0 0 1].

item.title: Go Daily Question 132
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

    name string
}

    var m map[person]int

Answer: 0

item.title: Go Daily Question 131
item.description:
Regarding channels, which of the following syntax is correct:

  • A. var ch chan int
  • B. ch := make(chan int)
  • C. <- ch
  • D. ch <-
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A, B, C

A declares variable ch of type chan int, but does not initialize it. B declares variable ch of type chan int, and initializes it. C reads from the channel, discarding the value. D is incorrect; writing to a channel requires a value.

item.title: Go Daily Question 080
item.description:
What code should be filled in at A and B below to ensure the result is printed successfully?

type S struct {
    m string
}

func f() *S {
    return __  //A
}

func main() {
    p := __    //B
    fmt.Println(p.m) //print "foo"
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A. &S{“foo”} B. *f() or f()

The f() function returns a pointer type, so & can be used to get the pointer to the struct. For B, if *f() is filled in, p is of type S; if f() is filled in, p is of type *S. However, in both cases, p.m can be used to access the struct member.

item.title: Go Daily Question 078
item.description:
What is the difference between the following two slice declarations? Which one is more preferable?

A. var a []int
B. a := []int{}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

A: Declares []int uninitialized, pointing to nil. B: Declares []int initialized, pointing to an empty array.

A can be declared globally. B can only be declared inside a function.

A and B theoretically occupy the same memory space. Note: An empty slice points to a fixed address, so no actual memory is allocated.

item.title: Go Daily Question 066
item.description:
How should A and B in the following code be modified to compile successfully?

func main() {
    var m map[string]int        //A
    m["a"] = 1
    if v := m["b"]; v != nil {  //B
        fmt.Println(v)
    }
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
func main() {
    m := make(map[string]int)
    m["a"] = 1
    if v,ok := m["b"]; ok {
        fmt.Println(v)
    }
}

At point A, map m is only declared, but no memory space is allocated. It cannot be directly assigned. make() needs to be used. It is generally recommended to initialize maps directly using make() or a literal.

item.title: Go Daily Question 062
item.description:
Which option can be filled in the blank in the following code?

func main() {
    var s1 []int
    var s2 = []int{}
    if __ == nil {
        fmt.Println("yes nil")
    }else{
        fmt.Println("no nil")
    }
}
  • A. s1
  • B. s2
  • C. Both s1 and s2

C s1 outputs “yes nil”. s2 outputs “no nil”.

item.title: Go Daily Question 039
item.description:
Regarding channels, which of the following syntax is correct:

A. var ch chan int
B. ch := make(chan int)
C. <- ch
D. ch <-
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: ABC

A and B both declare a channel; C reads from a channel; Writing to a channel must include a value, so D is incorrect.

item.title: Go Daily Question 011
item.description:
Difference between new() and make()

🔑 Answer Analysis:

new(T) allocates zeroed memory for a new value of type T and returns its address (a pointer), i.e., a value of type *T. In other words, it returns a pointer to a newly allocated, zero-valued T. It is suitable for value types, such as arrays and structs.

make(T, args) returns an initialized value of type T, which is not the zero value of type T, nor is it a pointer *T; it is a reference to an initialized T. make() is only applicable to slices, maps, and channels.
